title: Hydrology
summary: Hydrology questions cluster around four topics: measuring rainfall over a catchment, converting rainfall to runoff, the unit hydrograph, and flood frequency. The unit hydrograph definition is examined almost every sitting and is almost always got wrong in the same way — its 'unit' is a depth of RAINFALL, not of time. For Nepal, note the monsoon dominance, the flow duration curve as the basis of run-of-river hydropower design, and GLOF as a design flood case that rainfall frequency analysis cannot capture.

sections.heading: The hydrological cycle, precipitation and its measurement
sections.body:
**The water balance equation** is the accounting framework for everything else:

> **P = R + E + T + I + ΔS**

(precipitation = runoff + evaporation + transpiration + infiltration + change in storage)

**Nepal's hydrology is dominated by the south-west monsoon (June to September)**, which delivers about **80%** of the annual rainfall. The consequences run through every water-resources decision in the country: rivers swing enormously between monsoon and dry season, run-of-river hydropower output falls sharply in winter, and irrigation depends on stored or diverted flow precisely when there is least of it.

**Orographic effect** is the second dominant feature: rainfall increases sharply with elevation on the windward slopes, so a catchment's rainfall varies far more with **altitude** than with horizontal distance — which is why gauge networks in the hills are hard to design and why the isohyetal method matters here more than in the plains.

**Measurement.** A **non-recording (Symons) gauge** gives a daily total; a **recording gauge** — **tipping bucket, weighing bucket or natural syphon (float)** type — gives the **mass curve** of rainfall against time, from which **intensity** is obtained. Intensity, not total, is what governs drain and culvert design, so recording gauges are essential for urban drainage.

**Mean rainfall over a catchment** — three methods, and the choice matters:

| Method | How | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Arithmetic mean** | Simple average of all gauges | **Uniform** rainfall, evenly spread gauges, flat terrain |
| **Thiessen polygon** | Each gauge **weighted by its polygon area**, formed by perpendicular bisectors | Non-uniform gauge spacing, **reasonably flat** terrain |
| **Isohyetal** | Areas between **contours of equal rainfall**, weighted | **The most accurate**, especially in **mountainous** terrain |

**Isohyetal is the right method for Nepal's hills**, because the analyst can draw the isohyets to reflect **orographic and aspect effects** using judgement and topography — information that a Thiessen polygon, which knows only gauge positions, cannot use.

**Estimating a missing record.** If the **normal annual rainfall** at the missing station is within **10%** of the surrounding stations, use the simple **station average**; otherwise use the **normal ratio method**:

> **P_x = (1/M) Σ [ (N_x/N_i) · P_i ]**

**Testing a record for consistency** uses the **double mass curve**: plot the cumulative rainfall at the suspect station against the cumulative mean of surrounding stations. A **change of slope** indicates an inconsistency — the gauge was moved, its exposure changed, or the observation practice altered — and the earlier record is corrected by the ratio of the slopes.

**Depth–area–duration (DAD) analysis** and **intensity–duration–frequency (IDF) curves** are the design outputs: an IDF curve gives the rainfall intensity for a chosen duration and return period, and is the direct input to the rational method.

sections.heading: Losses — evaporation, evapotranspiration and infiltration
sections.body:
**Evaporation** is measured directly by a **Class A pan** (or IS pan), and converted by a **pan coefficient of about 0.7** to give lake evaporation — the pan being small, shallow and more responsive to air temperature than a real water body.

**Estimation methods:**

| Method | Basis |
|---|---|
| **Penman** | **Energy balance + aerodynamic (mass transfer)** — the most rigorous |
| Meyer, Rohwer | Mass transfer, empirical |
| Water budget | Balance of a reservoir |
| **Blaney–Criddle** | Temperature-based, for **evapotranspiration** |
| Thornthwaite, Hargreaves | Temperature-based |
| **FAO Penman–Monteith** | The modern reference method for ET₀ |

**Penman's method is the answer to "which is most rigorous"** because it combines both the energy available to evaporate water and the capacity of the air to remove it — the two physical requirements. Temperature-only methods work because temperature correlates with radiation, but they fail where wind or humidity is unusual.

**Evapotranspiration = evaporation + transpiration**, and the crop-specific value is

> **ET_crop = K_c × ET₀**

where **ET₀** is the reference (potential) evapotranspiration and **K_c** the crop coefficient, which varies through the crop's growth stages — small at establishment, peaking at full canopy, falling at maturity.

**Reducing reservoir evaporation** (a genuine problem in arid regions, less so in Nepal): wind breaks, floating covers, chemical films of **cetyl alcohol**, and — most effectively — designing for **greater depth and less surface area**.

**Infiltration** is the entry of water into the soil surface, at a rate that **decreases with time** as the soil wets up:

> **Horton's equation: f = f_c + (f₀ − f_c) e^{−kt}**

starting at the initial capacity f₀ and decaying to the **constant final capacity f_c**, which approaches the saturated permeability.

**Measurement:** the **double-ring infiltrometer** (the outer ring prevents lateral spreading from distorting the inner measurement) and **rainfall simulators**. At catchment scale, infiltration is inferred from **rainfall and runoff records** rather than measured.

**Infiltration indices** — used to separate rainfall excess from loss in a storm:

| Index | Definition |
|---|---|
| **φ-index** | The **constant loss rate** which, subtracted from the rainfall hyetograph, leaves a volume equal to the observed runoff |
| **W-index** | More refined — excludes **interception and depression storage**, so W ≤ φ |

The **φ-index is a lumped device, not a physical infiltration rate**: it absorbs interception, depression storage and evaporation as well as true infiltration. That is precisely why it is useful — it is the single number that makes the rainfall–runoff volumes balance.

**Factors affecting infiltration and runoff:**

| Increases runoff | Reduces runoff |
|---|---|
| **High rainfall intensity** | High infiltration capacity (sand, gravel) |
| **Steep slopes** | **Vegetation and forest cover** |
| **Impervious surfaces** (urbanisation) | Depression storage, ponds |
| **Saturated or frozen ground** | Dry, cracked soil (initially) |
| Compacted soil | Deep permeable soil |

**Urbanisation** is the most consequential of these for design: paving a catchment raises the **peak** flow and **shortens the time to peak**, so an existing drain sized for rural conditions is overwhelmed twice over. That is why storm drainage must be designed for the **future** land use, not the present one.

sections.heading: Runoff estimation and the unit hydrograph
sections.body:
**The rational method** — for **small** catchments:

> **Q = C I A / 3.6**   (Q in m³/s, I in mm/h, A in km²)

| Runoff coefficient C | Surface |
|---|---|
| **0.05 – 0.30** | Cultivated land, lawns, flat sandy soil |
| 0.30 – 0.50 | Suburban, gravel |
| 0.50 – 0.70 | Dense residential |
| **0.70 – 0.95** | **Paved, roofs, asphalt** |

**Its assumptions are strict**, and questions test them: the rainfall is **uniform over the whole catchment** and **constant for a duration equal to the time of concentration**, the coefficient C is constant, and the return period of the peak flow equals that of the rainfall. These hold only for **small** catchments — conventionally **under about 50 km²**.

**Time of concentration t_c** is the time for runoff to travel from the hydraulically most remote point to the outlet. The design storm duration is taken **equal to t_c**, because that is the duration giving the maximum peak: a shorter storm does not engage the whole catchment, and a longer one has a lower intensity. **Kirpich's formula** gives t_c from length and slope.

**The hydrograph** is a plot of discharge against time at a point, with three limbs — the **rising limb**, the **crest**, and the **recession (falling) limb** — and it comprises **direct runoff (surface + interflow)** plus **base flow** from groundwater.

**Base flow separation** methods: the **straight line**, the **fixed base length**, and the **variable slope** method. **N (days) = 0.83 A^{0.2}** gives the time from the peak to the end of direct runoff, with A in km².

**The unit hydrograph — the most examined item in hydrology, and the one most often misdefined:**

> A **unit hydrograph** is the **direct runoff hydrograph resulting from ONE UNIT DEPTH (1 cm) of effective rainfall falling uniformly over the entire catchment at a uniform rate within a SPECIFIED DURATION**.

**The unit is a depth of RAINFALL, not of time.** A 6-hour unit hydrograph and a 12-hour unit hydrograph are **different hydrographs of the same 1 cm** of rainfall excess — the duration is a label attached to the UH, not the unit itself. Answering that the unit refers to time, or to duration, is the standard error.

**Its three assumptions:**

| Assumption | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Time invariance** | The same storm produces the same hydrograph whenever it occurs |
| **Linearity (proportionality)** | 2 cm of excess produces ordinates **twice** as large, at the **same** times |
| **Superposition** | Hydrographs from successive rainfall blocks **add**, offset in time |

The **linearity assumption is the one that fails in reality** — catchments respond non-linearly, especially at extremes — which is why the unit hydrograph is applied within a limited range of storm magnitudes and why modern practice uses distributed models for extremes.

**Derived hydrographs:**

| Type | Derived by |
|---|---|
| UH of a **different duration** (integer multiple) | **Superposition** of lagged copies |
| UH of **any** duration | Via the **S-curve** (S-hydrograph), the response to continuous rainfall |
| **Instantaneous UH (IUH)** | Duration tending to zero — the catchment's pure impulse response |
| **Synthetic UH** | From **catchment characteristics** where no gauged data exists — **Snyder's** method, SCS dimensionless UH |

The **synthetic unit hydrograph** matters greatly in Nepal, where most catchments are **ungauged**: Snyder's method estimates the basin lag, peak and time base from the main stream length, the length to the centroid, and regional coefficients.

**Flood routing** predicts how a flood wave changes as it moves through a channel or reservoir:

| Method | Applies to |
|---|---|
| **Muskingum** | **Channel** routing — storage depends on both inflow and outflow |
| **Modified Puls / level pool** | **Reservoir** routing — storage depends on outflow only |

A reservoir **attenuates** the peak and **delays** it, which is the quantitative basis of flood control storage.

sections.heading: Flood frequency, flow duration and groundwater
sections.body:
**Return period (recurrence interval) T** is the average interval between events equalling or exceeding a given magnitude, so the annual probability is **P = 1/T**.

**The most misunderstood point in hydrology:** a **100-year flood has a 1% chance in ANY single year** — it is **not** "one flood per century", and two can occur in consecutive years without contradiction.

**Risk over a design life:**

> **Risk = 1 − (1 − 1/T)^n**  over n years

A worked case: over a **50-year** design life, the risk of exceeding the **100-year** flood is 1 − 0.99⁵⁰ = **39%**. That is why long-lived and high-consequence structures use long return periods:

| Structure | Typical design return period |
|---|---|
| Urban storm drain | **2 – 5 years** |
| Road culvert, minor bridge | 25 – 50 years |
| Major bridge | **100 years** |
| Barrage, weir | 100 – 500 years |
| **Large dam spillway** | **1000 years to the Probable Maximum Flood** |

The **PMF** is used for a large dam because the consequence of failure is catastrophic and no probability of exceedance is acceptable.

**Frequency analysis** fits a distribution to the annual maximum series:

| Distribution | Note |
|---|---|
| **Gumbel (EV1)** | The classical choice for annual maxima |
| **Log-Pearson Type III** | Standard in the USA; handles skew |
| Log-normal | — |
| **Plotting positions** | **Weibull P = m/(N+1)**, California, Hazen |

The **general frequency formula**:

> **x_T = x̄ + K σ**

with K the frequency factor for the chosen distribution and return period.

**A caution on extrapolation.** A 40-year record extrapolated to a 1000-year flood is a very long reach, and the confidence limits are wide. Reporting a single number without its uncertainty is misleading, and the professional practice is to state the confidence band and to cross-check against **regional flood formulae** (Dickens, Ryves, Inglis, or a regional envelope curve) and against **historical flood marks**.

**The flow duration curve** plots discharge against the **percentage of time it is equalled or exceeded**:

| Feature | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Flat** curve | Well-regulated flow — large groundwater or snowmelt contribution |
| **Steep** curve | A **flashy** river; needs storage to be useful |
| **Q₄₀** | The conventional **design flow for run-of-river hydropower** in Nepal |
| **Q₉₅ – Q₁₀₀** | **Firm (primary) power** — available almost all the time |

The FDC is the single most useful diagram in Nepali hydropower planning: the **installed capacity** is fixed from a high-flow exceedance (typically Q₄₀), while the **firm energy** that commands the higher tariff is fixed at the low-flow end.

**The mass curve (Rippl) method** sizes **storage**: plot cumulative inflow against time, draw tangents of the demand slope at the peaks, and the **maximum vertical intercept** between tangent and curve is the storage required. It also identifies the **critical drought period**, which is the real design case.

**Groundwater.**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Aquifer** | A formation that **stores and transmits** usable water |
| **Aquiclude** | Stores but does **not transmit** (clay) |
| **Aquifuge** | Neither stores nor transmits (massive rock) |
| **Unconfined (water table) aquifer** | Upper surface is the water table, at atmospheric pressure |
| **Confined (artesian) aquifer** | Between impermeable layers; water rises above the aquifer top when tapped |
| **Specific yield** | Water **drained by gravity** ÷ total volume |
| **Specific retention** | Water **retained** against gravity |
| **Porosity** | = specific yield + specific retention |

That last identity is worth noting: **a clay has high porosity but almost no specific yield**, which is why it holds a great deal of water and gives up almost none — the reason porosity alone never indicates a good aquifer.

**Well hydraulics** — steady radial flow to a well:

> **Unconfined (Dupuit): Q = πk(H² − h²)/ln(R/r)**
> **Confined (Thiem): Q = 2πkb(H − h)/ln(R/r)**

**Specific capacity** = discharge per unit drawdown, the practical measure of a well's productivity. **Interference** occurs where the cones of depression of adjacent wells overlap, reducing the yield of both — which is why well spacing is a design decision, not an administrative one.

**GLOF — glacial lake outburst flood** — deserves separate mention as a design case **peculiar to Nepal's high mountains**. A moraine-dammed glacial lake breaches and releases a flood of very large peak and very short duration. It is **not captured by rainfall frequency analysis**, because its cause is not rainfall at all. Hydropower schemes, bridges and settlements in the high Himalaya must therefore assess GLOF risk **separately**, from glacial lake inventories and dam-break modelling — and the risk is rising as glaciers retreat.

formulas.label: Water balance
formulas.expression: P = R + E + T + I + ΔS
formulas.note: The accounting framework for all catchment hydrology.

formulas.label: Rational method
formulas.expression: Q = C I A / 3.6     (Q in m³/s, I in mm/h, A in km²)
formulas.note: Small catchments only (< ~50 km²). Storm duration is taken equal to the time of concentration.

formulas.label: Horton's infiltration equation
formulas.note: Infiltration capacity decays from f₀ to the constant final rate f_c.

formulas.label: Missing rainfall (normal ratio method)
formulas.note: Used when the normal annual rainfall differs by more than 10% from the surrounding stations.

formulas.label: Unit hydrograph definition
formulas.expression: Direct runoff from 1 cm of effective rainfall, uniform over the catchment, in a SPECIFIED duration
formulas.note: The UNIT is a depth of RAINFALL, not of time. Assumes time invariance, linearity and superposition.

formulas.label: Base flow separation time
formulas.note: Time from the peak to the end of direct runoff.

formulas.label: Return period and risk
formulas.note: A 100-year flood has a 1% chance in ANY year. Over 50 years the risk of exceedance is 39%.

formulas.label: Frequency analysis
formulas.expression: x_T = x̄ + K σ ;   Weibull plotting position P = m/(N + 1)
formulas.note: K is the frequency factor for the chosen distribution (Gumbel, Log-Pearson III).

formulas.label: Steady radial flow to a well
formulas.expression: Unconfined: Q = πk(H² − h²)/ln(R/r).   Confined: Q = 2πkb(H − h)/ln(R/r).
formulas.note: Specific capacity = discharge per unit drawdown. Porosity = specific yield + specific retention.

formulas.label: Evapotranspiration
formulas.note: K_c varies through the crop growth stages. Penman combines energy balance with an aerodynamic term.
